albums.blurb: Jimmy Smith did more than anyone to make the Hammond B-3 organ a lead jazz instrument, and this set comes from a single April 1960 session at Rudy Van Gelder's New Jersey studio that also produced its companion album, Midnight Special. Cut with Stanley Turrentine on tenor saxophone, Kenny Burrell on guitar, and Donald Bailey on drums, it distills the relaxed, blues-drenched small-group sound of Smith's final Blue Note years, shortly before his move to Verve.
albums.reception: The album is cited in the book 1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die, and its session is remembered as the first to draw wide attention to tenor saxophonist Stanley Turrentine.

albums.blurb: Stevens's fifth album and the second entry in his famously abandoned plan to record one album for each U.S. state, following 2003's Michigan. Its 22 tracks fold banjo, woodwinds, choir, and chamber-orchestra arrangements around Illinois history and geography — Chicago, the Sears Tower, John Wayne Gacy Jr. — and it remains the centerpiece of his orchestral folk period.
albums.reception: Illinois was Metacritic's best-reviewed album of 2005 and later appeared on best-of-the-decade lists from NPR, Paste, and Rolling Stone.

albums.blurb: Shuggie Otis, son of R&B bandleader Johnny Otis, was a guitar prodigy who recorded with his father's band as a teenager and wrote "Strawberry Letter 23," later a hit for the Brothers Johnson. This third album — self-produced, with Otis playing most of the instruments and working with an early drum machine — closed out his original recording run: Epic dropped him afterward, and he released no new studio album for decades.
albums.reception: It reached number 181 on the Billboard 200, its title track hit number 56 on the R&B singles chart in 1975, and the 2001 reissue on David Byrne's Luaka Bop label established it as a cult classic.
